description: We are three computer science students passionate about software and space. For this challenge, we’re building an interactive tool where astronauts track vitals like heart rate, blood pressure, sleep and mood, with color-coded charts and a clickable body map. We’ve got the coding covered, so we’re looking for teammates with health/biomedical knowledge, UI/UX or graphic design, animation, and storytelling skills. Let’s build it together!
summary: Crew Health Monitor is a browser dashboard that helps astronauts read their own health data when the flight surgeon is far away. A clickable body figure shows six body systems in green, yellow or red, and seven indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise) are charted against alert thresholds, each with a plain-language explanation that cites NASA Human Research Program evidence. A Health Interpreter explains active alerts, links problems that started together and gives a step-by-step checklist. Early drift flags a slow shift away from a crew member's own baseline even while every reading is still nominal. On long missions, crews must notice problems early and act without immediate medical help; the app turns scattered numbers into one clear picture. It runs in the browser with no backend, works offline, and uses simulated data for three fictional crew members.
details:
What it does. Crew Health Monitor is a single-screen health console for a space crew. A body figure shows six body systems, each in the colour of its worst indicator, so a problem is visible in one second. Seven indicator tiles and trend charts (24 hours, 7 days or the whole mission) show green, yellow and red threshold zones, with a readings table for exact values. A Health Interpreter gives a plain-language summary of what is out of range, which problems started together and may be linked, and a numbered "What to do now" checklist with a source for each step where one exists. Early drift compares sleep, mood, heart rate and body temperature with each crew member's own first 7 mission days and flags a slow shift even while every reading is still nominal; the app calls it a pattern worth reviewing, never a diagnosis. Every indicator has an about panel: what it is, why it is monitored, how spaceflight affects it, its thresholds and where each threshold comes from.

How it works. A React web app built with Vite and Chart.js. A deterministic simulator generates readings with daily rhythms, meals, exercise, sleep and scripted events: a fever, a stretch of sleep loss and a quiet drift. Status compares each reading with its thresholds. Early drift computes a personal baseline (mean and standard deviation of the first 7 days) and flags 2 or more indicators that sit at least 1.5 standard deviations on the unfavourable side for 3 days in a row; these numbers are team choices for the demo, not clinical criteria. There is no backend: data stays in the browser and the app works offline. Try it live: https://erenbaris838.github.io/crew-health-monitor/

Benefits and creativity. One glance shows who needs attention and why. Instead of a red light, the app explains the situation in plain language and gives step-by-step actions a crew member without medical training can follow, and it compares each person with their own normal, catching a quiet change before any alarm. Every claim links to its source, and every threshold says whether it comes from NASA, a clinical reference or the team. Status is always shown by icon shape and word as well as colour, so colour-blind users can read it; there are day and night modes and keyboard access.

What we hope to achieve. Next we want smart-garment sensors woven into clothing, cabin data such as CO2, noise and light to explain root causes, personal alarm limits and heart-rate-variability trends.

Tools, languages and software. JavaScript (React JSX), HTML and CSS; React, Vite, Chart.js, react-chartjs-2 and the Atkinson Hyperlegible Next font; Node.js and npm; GitHub and GitHub Pages; Claude (Anthropic) as the SI tool; Playwright and FFmpeg to capture and encode the demo video. No hardware.

Honest about sources and SI. NASA Human Research Program evidence reports describe the risks but, in the sources we found, set no alarm limits for most vital signs, so every threshold in the app is labelled with its basis: NASA source, clinical reference or team-defined. All code and written content were made with SI tools (Claude, Anthropic); this is disclosed in the README, in every source file header, in the package metadata, in the app footer and with a visible watermark on the demo video.
